questions.question: You flip production yourself in this setup — on a real team, who gets that authority, and how many people would need it?
questions.why: The morning-report slide says only the speaker can flip production, which is a single point of control a team would need to redesign.

questions.question: With forty-five possible forks for one bug, who decides which ones actually get run first?
questions.why: The fork-tree slide shows the branching but never says who prioritizes among that many options.

questions.question: Is 65% on live lots good enough to ship to real users, and what's the target number before you'd call this done?
questions.why: The speaker calls two-in-three 'not done, but measurable' without naming the bar for actually shipping.

questions.question: The coordinator is your strongest model judging your own lanes — on a team, who plays that role, and can a junior PM own it?
questions.why: Orchestration is described as one person's coordinator session, which doesn't obviously map to a multi-person team.

questions.question: Thirty minutes a day is your estimate and doesn't count morning review time — what's the real daily time cost end to end?
questions.why: The cost line explicitly excludes review time from the headline number, which looks like it undercounts total effort.

questions.question: A hundred experiments in two weeks — was that one person working full time, or could a team hit that pace part-time?
questions.why: The experiment count is given without any sense of how many people or how much focus it required.

questions.question: Who writes the kill bar before a run — you alone, or could someone else on a team set that gate?
questions.why: Kill lines are shown as the speaker's own judgment call with no mention of shared ownership.

questions.question: The persona panel said DONE but your own phone said no — what changed in your process so that gap doesn't happen again?
questions.why: The persona-gate story ends in a false pass caught by luck the next morning, which raises doubt about the gate's reliability.

questions.question: What's the actual first thing a product manager who doesn't run worktrees should do Monday morning?
questions.why: The starter kit is aimed at engineering-style workflows and doesn't spell out a PM's entry point.

questions.question: Beyond the $9 in labeling calls, what does the Claude Max subscription itself cost, and does that scale if a whole team runs this?
questions.why: The cost slide highlights the small metered spend but treats the subscription cost as a given, not a line item to budget.
